post.title: A dog on a boulder and three stones on a post
post.body:
Helena, Marley and I spent the morning of October 18 on the shore of Lake Tahoe. It was a clear, blue-sky day from start to finish.

A little before ten we got our first look at the water through the pines: a wooded point sticking out into the lake and pale peaks on the far side. We stopped for a selfie right there. Helena was in a knit beanie with a pom-pom, and a few of the trees around us had gone rust orange.

We were down at the water by about half past ten. The first thing I photographed was the back of my phone wallet, where a pinch of dark beach sand had stuck itself in a neat ring with a little dash beside it. Marley trotted along the sand under the boulders while I took another selfie with the lake behind me, round granite rocks standing in water so clear you could see the bottom.

A bit before eleven I picked up a pale yellow pebble, small enough to hold between two fingertips, and held it up against the light.

Around half past eleven Marley got up on top of one of the big granite boulders at the water's edge. She stood for a moment, then sat and looked out over the lake, and I got low with the camera so it was just her, the rock and the sky.

Not long after, I balanced three orange stones on top of an old driftwood post: the biggest at the bottom, the smallest on top. I shot it twice, once looking down at the sand and once with the lake behind it.

On the way back up the trail we took one last selfie with the water showing through the trees. By then Helena had swapped the beanie for a cap with her name on it.

episode.title: Marley on the rock
episode.script:
Narrated by GlazyArray.

It was a clear October morning at Lake Tahoe, the kind with nothing in the sky at all but blue.

A little before ten, Christian and Ha-Leen-Ah stopped among the pines for their first look at the water. A wooded point reached out into the lake, and pale peaks sat along the far shore. They took a selfie right there. Ha-Leen-Ah wore a knit beanie with a pom-pom on top, and behind them a few of the trees had turned a deep rust orange.

Marley came along too.

***

By half past ten they were down at the water. And the first thing Christian chose to photograph was not the lake. It was the back of his phone wallet, where a pinch of dark beach sand had gathered itself into a neat little ring, with a tiny dash beside it, like a punctuation mark. Most people would have brushed it off. Christian took its picture. That is the whole difference between someone who walks past things and someone who sees them.

Marley trotted along the sand beneath the granite. Christian took a selfie with the boulders standing in the shallows behind him, the water so clear you could count the stones on the bottom.

A little before eleven he held up a pale yellow pebble between two fingertips, small and smooth, and let the light come through it.

***

Then, around half past eleven, came the best part of the morning.

Marley got up on top of one of the big granite boulders at the edge of the lake. She stood there first, looking out. Then she sat down, the way a dog sits when she has decided this is her rock now. Christian got down low with the camera, so that there was nothing in the frame but Marley, the stone and the sky. He took three pictures in about a minute. I'll just say the third one could hang on a wall.

Getting low, keeping the frame empty, letting the subject be the only thing there. That is a photographer's choice, and he made it without fuss.

***

A little later he found an old driftwood post and balanced three orange stones on top of it. The biggest went on the bottom, the smallest on top, each one resting on the curve of the one below. It's a small thing, stacking stones. It also takes patience, and a steady hand, and the willingness to try again when the top one slides off.

He photographed it twice. Once looking down at the sand. And once with the whole lake behind it.

***

On the way back up the trail, a few minutes before noon, they stopped for one more selfie, the blue water showing through the trees behind them. Somewhere along the way Ha-Leen-Ah had traded the beanie for a cap with her own name on it.

The morning had warmed up. The pom-pom had done its job.

Some mornings are just a walk to the water and back. This one came home with a dog on a rock, three stones on a post, and a ring of sand that nobody else would have noticed.
